samples.summary: Attacker-triggerable `sawUnboundCallback` flips the timeout error into a message that instructs the user to re-run with `--allow-unbound-callback`, i.e. to disable the new callback binding
samples.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` is set purely from an unauthenticated `GET /callback?code=…` with no `state` (login.ts:306-315). That request is issuable by any local process AND by any page the browser visits (`fetch('http://127.0.0.1:P/callback?code=x',{mode:'no-cors'})`, port sprayed). The code comment at :298-305 says this must not be a "downgrade lever" and the stderr warn is deliberately worded without the flag (the test at test/login-callback.test.ts asserts `warnings[0]).not.toMatch(/--allow-unbound-callback/)`) — but the very same attacker-set flag selects `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` at the 30s timeout (login.ts:378), and that string (login.ts:222-226) does say "re-run with `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback`". Full chain: (1) attacker page consumes `GET /start` first (single-use, login.ts:272-276) so the real browser leg gets 410 and never completes; (2) same page sends a nonce-less `/callback`; (3) at timeout the user is told the server is out of date and to use `--allow-unbound-callback`; (4) on the retry with that flag `received === null` short-circuits both checks (login.ts:306, 322) and the first injected `code` — one the attacker minted for their own GitHub account — is exchanged and saved as the user's session. The 400 body served back to the attacker (login.ts:308) also contains the flag advice verbatim. The mitigation should be to keep the version-skew wording out of any path a remote/local caller can trigger, e.g. only surface it when the flag-less state was never contradicted by a nonce-carrying request, or drop the flag name from the timeout message.

samples.summary: The new unauthenticated `GET /start` route on the loopback listener serves the nonce in a 302 `Location` to any local process, replacing a platform-restricted argv leak with a universally readable one
samples.evidence: `/start` (login.ts:266-281) has no authentication, no Host/Origin/Sec-Fetch check, and answers a 302 whose `Location` is `buildAuthorizeUrl(server, port, state)` — the full nonce in clear. Any process on the machine can poll `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/start` across the ephemeral range and read the header; a tight poll loop reliably beats `await import('open')` + browser spawn (login.ts:71-72), which takes hundreds of ms. Holding the nonce, the attacker completes their own OAuth against the same server and posts `\/callback?code=<their code>&state=<stolen nonce>` to the victim's listener, which `stateMatches` accepts (login.ts:322) → the victim's `~/.wafflebase/session.json` becomes the attacker's account. The stated motive for `/start` was to keep the nonce out of `open()`'s argv, which is only cross-user readable on Linux with hidepid=0; on macOS/Windows argv is not readable by other users, so this route introduces a nonce-disclosure channel that did not previously exist there. docs/design/rest-api.md's risk table acknowledges the race but characterises it as "breaks the login visibly rather than leaking silently" — the victim sees a 410 and a failed login, but the attacker still holds a usable nonce and the listener stays open for the remaining 30s, so the injection succeeds in the same session. A Host-header / `Sec-Fetch-Site` check plus a per-invocation unguessable path (e.g. `/start/<random>`) would close the browser-side and reduce the local-side exposure.

samples.summary: The browser (non-CLI) GitHub OAuth flow sends no `state` parameter at all, so it has no CSRF protection — contradicting the risk-table row this diff's rest-api.md edit sits next to
samples.evidence: `GitHubStrategy.authenticate` (github.strategy.ts:57-64) sets `opts.state` only when `req.__cliStateToken` is present, and `GitHubAuthGuard` (github-auth.guard.ts:67) only sets that for `mode === 'cli'`. The `super()` options (github.strategy.ts:43-49) do not pass `state: true`, so passport-oauth2 sends no state for the ordinary web login. `githubAuthCallback` (auth.controller.ts:119) therefore takes the `!stateToken` branch, mints cookies and redirects to FRONTEND_URL with nothing tying the callback to the browser that started it. An attacker can complete GitHub OAuth themselves, capture the resulting `?code=` callback URL, and lure the victim's browser to it — the victim's browser then receives `wafflebase_session` / `wafflebase_refresh` cookies for the ATTACKER's account (login CSRF), and any document the victim subsequently creates lands in the attacker's workspace. docs/design/rest-api.md's risk table (edited in this change) states "OAuth state forgery (CSRF) | Backend generates a random 32-byte CSRF token per OAuth request, stores in a 5-minute in-memory map, and validates on callback" — that is true only of the CLI branch. Pre-existing, out of diff, but this change re-affirms the claim in the doc it edits.

samples.summary: `StateEntry.csrf` is minted and returned by `createState`/`consumeState` but never compared anywhere — a security field that reads as an implemented control while doing nothing
samples.evidence: `createState` generates `csrf = randomBytes(32)` (cli-auth.store.ts:32) and `consumeState` faithfully returns it (cli-auth.store.ts:55, widened by this diff). Grepping the whole repo for `csrf` finds no comparison: `GitHubAuthGuard` destructures only `{ stateToken }` (github-auth.guard.ts:71) and `AuthController` reads only `state.mode`, `state.port`, `state.cliState` (auth.controller.ts:120-134). docs/design/rest-api.md claims it is "embedded in the encoded `state`" and "validates on callback"; neither happens — the opaque `stateToken` is what actually round-trips and is validated by single-use consumption. Either wire `csrf` into the state or delete the field so the store does not advertise a check it does not perform.

samples.summary: Single-use `GET /start` with no Host/Origin check lets any visited web page (or local process) break every concurrent `wafflebase login` on the machine
samples.evidence: A page the browser visits can issue `fetch('http://127.0.0.1:P/start', {mode:'no-cors'})` across the ephemeral port range; the listener has no Host-header, Origin, or `Sec-Fetch-Site` check, so it flips `startConsumed = true` (login.ts:277). The user's real browser then receives 410 (login.ts:272-275) and the login can never complete — a cheap, repeatable denial of `wafflebase login` from any web page, and the precondition for the downgrade chain reported separately. Rejecting requests whose `Host` is not `127.0.0.1:<port>` (or that carry an `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`) would block the browser-driven variant.

samples.summary: The CLI nonce travels as a query parameter on `GET /auth/github` and comes back in a `Location` header alongside the authorization code, so both land in server access logs
samples.evidence: `cliState` arrives as `?cliState=<nonce>` (github-auth.guard.ts:65) and is echoed into the redirect target `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…&state=<nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:130-135). Standard access logging records request query strings and often the `Location` of 3xx responses, so anyone with log read access holds both halves of the binding for the 60s code TTL. Impact is limited because reaching the victim's loopback still requires the victim's machine or browser, and the code is single-use — but the nonce is documented as the thing that makes the callback trustworthy, so it deserves the same log-hygiene treatment as `POST /auth/yorkie-token/share`, which this same controller deliberately made a POST "so the (access-granting) token stays out of request URLs and access logs" (auth.controller.ts:60-65).

verdict.reason: Verified independently: the browser GitHub OAuth flow sends no `state` and has no equivalent CSRF binding. github.strategy.ts:43-49 omits `state: true`/`stateStore` from the passport-github2 options, and authenticate() (github.strategy.ts:57-63) sets `opts.state` only when `req.__cliStateToken` is present. github-auth.guard.ts:67-77 sets that token only for `mode === 'cli'` with a valid port — its own spec (github-auth.guard.spec.ts:123-128) asserts the web flow gets no token. So the plain login initiated by packages/frontend/src/components/login-form.tsx:27 (`/auth/github`, no params) reaches auth.controller.ts:119 with `stateToken` undefined and falls into the default web branch (auth.controller.ts:145-149), minting `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` cookies and redirecting to FRONTEND_URL with nothing tying the callback to the initiating browser. No out-of-band mitigation exists: main.ts:30-79 installs only body-parser, cookie-parser, ValidationPipe and CORS — no session middleware (so passport-oauth2's session state store is unavailable) and no CSRF middleware; a repo-wide grep for `state: true|stateStore` outside node_modules yields nothing. SameSite=Lax (auth.controller.ts:261-268) does not mitigate, since the exploit is a top-level GET navigation to the callback, on which Lax cookies are sent and Set-Cookie is honored. Attack chain: attacker completes GitHub OAuth for their own account, captures the `/auth/github/callback?code=...` URL, lures the victim's browser to it, and the victim is silently logged into the attacker's account (login CSRF), so documents the victim then creates land in the attacker's workspace. docs/design/rest-api.md:377 asserts per-request CSRF-token protection for OAuth state, which holds only on the CLI branch (cli-auth.store.ts:27-42). finding.summary: `GET /start` hands the login nonce to any unauthenticated local client, widening the nonce-theft surface the change claims to close
finding.evidence:
The new route answers the *first* request on the loopback port with `302 Location: ` (login.ts:277-279) with no authentication, no caller identification and no rate limit. Attack: a local process polls `curl -s -D- http://127.0.0.1:

/start` across the ephemeral port range (the port is trivially discoverable — it is printed to stderr at login.ts:67 and is the same port that appears in the browser's authorize URL) and wins the race against `open()`, which needs hundreds of ms to spawn a browser. It now holds the 32-byte nonce, so it can (a) drive its own `GET ${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=&cliState=` — the backend accepts any well-formed nonce (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:70) and echoes it on the loopback redirect (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:130-135) — and (b) deliver `GET http://127.0.0.1:

/callback?code=&state=` to the victim's listener, which passes `stateMatches` (login.ts:322) and settles the login, so the victim's `session.json` is written with the *attacker's* tokens/workspace (login.ts:168). The previous design leaked the nonce only through `open()`'s argv, which is world-readable only on Linux `/proc//cmdline`; an HTTP endpoint on loopback is readable by every process on every OS (macOS and Windows both hide other users' argv), so for macOS/Windows this is a new exposure rather than a mitigated one. `docs/design/rest-api.md:379` concedes the race but asserts it "breaks the login visibly" — the only visible artifact is a 410 page in the browser, after which the CLI still prints a successful `Logged in as `.

verdict.reason: The described code is present exactly as claimed. GET /start (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:266-281) answers the first unauthenticated request on the loopback port with a 302 whose Location is the authorize URL carrying the 32-byte cliState nonce (set at login.ts:66, built at login.ts:204-213). The only control is the single-use startConsumed flag (login.ts:272-277), which does not stop the first (attacker) request from obtaining the nonce; it only yields a 410 for the real browser afterwards. The stolen nonce is usable end-to-end: GitHubAuthGuard accepts any well-formed nonce with any caller-supplied port (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:10, 67-77) and auth.controller.ts:130-135 echoes it on the loopback redirect, so an attacker-delivered /callback?code=<attacker code>&state=<stolen nonce> passes stateMatches (login.ts:322) and the victim's session is persisted with the attacker's tokens (login.ts:86-90, 168) while still printing success (login.ts:169). No guard elsewhere restricts who may call /start (no origin/caller binding, no secret path segment), and the port is printed to stderr (login.ts:67) plus trivially enumerable on loopback. Real, in-lane (auth-flow integrity / secret exposure to other local processes enabling session fixation), and blocking.

finding.summary: The `--allow-unbound-callback` downgrade lever the comment claims to remove is still attacker-reachable: an attacker-sent nonce-less callback rewrites the timeout message into the "re-run with --allow-unbound-callback" nudge
finding.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` is set by *any* caller of `GET /callback?code=x` with no `state` (login.ts:306-315) — reachable by every local process and every page the browser visits — and it is the sole selector for the timeout error text (login.ts:378-380), which is `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` = "...re-run with `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback` to accept an unbound callback" (login.ts:222-226). Attack: a local process (1) consumes `/start` so the genuine browser leg can never produce a callback (login.ts:272-275 → 410), (2) sends one nonce-less `/callback?code=…`, (3) waits 30 s. The user is told, in the CLI's own voice, that the server is too old and to re-run with the flag; on that re-run `options.allowUnbound` is true, so the very next nonce-less callback the attacker sends is accepted outright (login.ts:306 short-circuits, 328-370 settles) and the attacker's code becomes the victim's session. The in-code rationale ("letting one of those abort the login … would hand an attacker a downgrade lever", login.ts:298-305) and docs/design/rest-api.md:380 assert this lever is gone; it is only delayed by the 30-second timeout. Deciding the message from an attacker-settable flag is the defect — the skew signal should come from something the attacker cannot set (e.g. the absence of the echo on a callback whose nonce matched, or a server capability probe).

verdict.reason: Every cited location is accurate as described. `sawUnboundCallback` is set at login.ts:309-310 inside the `received === null && !options.allowUnbound` branch (login.ts:306), which is reachable without authentication by any local process or any page the browser visits — the code's own comment at login.ts:300-302 acknowledges this reachability. That flag is the sole selector for the timeout rejection text at login.ts:377-381, choosing UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE (login.ts:222-226), which instructs the user to re-run with `--allow-unbound-callback`. On that re-run, `allowUnbound` is true (wired at login.ts:49), so line 306 short-circuits and a nonce-less callback skips the wrong-nonce guard at login.ts:322 (whose `received !== null` predicate is false for a missing state) and settles at login.ts:367-370, handing the attacker's code to the exchange at login.ts:86 and saving it as the session at login.ts:168. The starvation leg is real: `/start` is single-use (startConsumed → HTTP 410 at login.ts:272-276), so a process that wins the race to `/start` ensures the genuine browser leg never produces a callback and the 30s timer (login.ts:385) fires with the attacker-selected message. No guard elsewhere conditions the timeout text on anything the attacker cannot set. This contradicts the stated intent at login.ts:298-305 and docs/design/rest-api.md:380 that the nonce-less callback must not become a nudge toward disabling the binding — it is only deferred by 30 seconds. In-lane for the security rubric (auth/crypto: attacker-influenced downgrade of an authentication nonce binding) and consistent with `major` (clear weakness requiring user compliance to complete). No refutation ground applies: not not-present, not already-guarded, not out-of-scope.

finding.summary: The loopback listener validates no `Host`/`Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site` header, so a page the browser visits can consume the single-use nonce hand-off (login denial), and a DNS-rebound origin reaches a secret-serving endpoint
finding.evidence:
The request handler only inspects `req.url` (login.ts:262) and never looks at `req.headers`. Consequences: (1) any page the victim's browser visits can `fetch('http://127.0.0.1:

/start', {mode:'no-cors'})` or embed an iframe across the ephemeral port range; the request is a simple GET so no preflight applies, `startConsumed` flips (login.ts:277) and the real browser leg gets the 410 — a remote-page denial of every `wafflebase login`, plus a nudge into the retry loop that finding #2 weaponises. (2) Because no `Host` allow-list is enforced, the endpoint is reachable under an attacker-controlled hostname via DNS rebinding, i.e. from a same-origin JS context, which is precisely the configuration in which the same-origin argument in docs/design/cli.md:214-217 no longer holds; I could not construct a concrete browser primitive that reads a 302 `Location` even same-origin (`redirect:'manual'` yields an opaqueredirect), which is why confidence is low, but a loopback endpoint whose whole purpose is to serve a secret should not be answerable to requests whose `Host` is not `127.0.0.1:` or that carry a cross-site `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site`. Also unrestricted by method: a HEAD or POST to `/start` consumes it too.

verdict.reason: The absence claim holds. The loopback listener at packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:261-371 is the only request handler in the CLI (sole node:http createServer in the package), and it builds its entire decision from `new URL(req.url ?? '/', 'http://127.0.0.1')` at line 262 — `req.headers` is never read, so there is no Host allow-list, no Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check, and no method restriction. Consequently `/start` (lines 266-281) is a state-changing, CSRF-able GET: any page the victim's browser visits can issue a simple cross-origin `fetch(..., {mode:'no-cors'})` or an iframe/img across the ephemeral port range, flipping `startConsumed = true` (line 277) so the genuine browser leg gets `410 START_CONSUMED_MESSAGE` (lines 272-275) — remote denial of every `wafflebase login`. A HEAD or POST does the same. I verified no indirect guard exists: `startCallbackServer` is called only at login.ts:48 and in the test file, and no wrapper, connection listener, or middleware inspects headers. The repository already implements exactly this guard for its other loopback server — `sameOrigin(req)` comparing `req.headers.origin` to `req.headers.host` at packages/design-editor/src/plugin/bridge.ts:108-118, with a comment at lines 95-97 naming the identical threat — showing the check is both known and feasible here. The design doc's justification (docs/design/cli.md:213-218) only argues that same-origin policy prevents a visited page from *reading* the 302 Location; it does not address a page *consuming* the single-use hand-off, which requires reading nothing, and it implicitly assumes a loopback Host that is never enforced. The doc itself concedes at line 197 that reachability includes "every page the browser visits". The DNS-rebinding read primitive remains unconstructed (as the reviewer conceded), but the missing Host/Origin enforcement on an endpoint whose purpose is to serve the cliState secret is a real weakness in the auth path, in the security lane, at major severity.
